newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Curfew in northwest Cameroon, gunmen kill gendarmes.
newsitem.headline: Curfew in northwest Cameroon, gunmen kill gendarmes.

text.p: The governor of Cameroon's volatile English-speaking North-west province on Sunday declared an indefinite overnight curfew after gunmen killed three gendarmes and a civilian in a spate of attacks.

Police blame the attacks on separatists in the province but a leading opposition party accused President Paul Biya and his government of stirring up trouble in the province with a view to postponing planned May elections there.
Governor Francis Fai Yengo placed the provincial capital Bamenda and the rest of the province under a 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew after a spate of attacks -- the latest early on Sunday.

Political sources reported a wave of arrests, including Lawrence Fomanbou, local representative of the National Union for Democracy and Progress (UNDP) of leading opposition politician Bello Bouba Maigari.
Police said gunmen killed a paramilitary gendarme guarding the state radio and television offices in Bamenda on Sunday.
The gunmen, who have been targeting security forces and public buildings, killed one gendarme in a Bamenda police post on Friday and one in Jakari in a similar attack on Thursday.
The fourth fatality was a civilian hit by a stray bullet in Bamenda during Friday's attack.
State radio has also reported attacks in Mbengwi and Kumbo.
The opposition Social Democratic Front of John Fru Ndi accused the government of dirty tricks.
"It is impossible for any separatist group to carry on such attacks in a province which is so much militarised," it said.

It accused the government of trying to foment an insurrection in the English-speaking North-west and South-west provinces before declaring a state of emergency there and ruling the provinces out of the election.
The government, which has made no formal comment on the attacks, has yet to announce a precise election date.
The May election will be the second parliamentary poll since Cameroon's sometimes turbulent transition to multi-party democracy began in 1990.
Part of the opposition boycotted the last legislative election in 1992. Biya supporters secured a majority then after allying with a minor party.

The government postponed this year's election from March after opposition party complaints that their militants had not had enough time to register. The opposition has demanded an independent national electoral commission.
Biya, who took over from independence president Ahmadou Ahidjo in 1982, faces a presidential election in October.
